items: Module = any directory holding `.tf` files. No manifest, no registration
Root module: the directory where you run `terraform apply`
Child module: one that another module calls via a `module` block
Modules are called, not imported — each block is a fresh instantiation
Child resources get a prefix: `module.vpc.aws_subnet.private[0]`
Two calls to one module = two address spaces, nothing shared
No provider scope: providers are inherited from the caller
Everything flattens into one plan and one state file

blocks.title: Standard Structure
items: `main.tf`, `variables.tf`, `outputs.tf`
`versions.tf`, `README.md`
`examples/` — docs and test target
`terraform init` downloads modules into `.terraform/modules/`
Changed a `source`? Re-run init or plan uses the cached copy
`.terraform/modules/modules.json` maps each call to its real path
Read that file when a "wrong version" mystery appears

blocks.text: A module has no state file. There is one state per root configuration, holding every child's resources.

blocks.title: Anti-definition
blocks.text: Not a package, not a class, not a function with side effects you can safely call twice. It is a value-level abstraction, not a runtime boundary.

items: No `default` at all = the variable is required
`default = null` = optional, and the module sees "not supplied"
`nullable = false` forbids passing null explicitly — a separate rule
`sensitive = true` redacts plan output only
`any` is the top source of confusing downstream errors
`optional(string, "eu-west-1")` inside `object()` gives per-attribute defaults
Needs Terraform 1.3+; before that callers passed full objects
Catches bad input at plan time, not halfway through apply
Many `validation` blocks allowed; each reports independently
One rule per block keeps the error message readable

blocks.title: Three Traps
items: `*.auto.tfvars` load alphabetically — later wins
`default` must be literal: no vars, resources, data
`TF_VAR_x` hits the root only; children get values from their block

blocks.title: Name For Intent
blocks.text: `enable_public_access` beats `create_igw_and_route`. The second name ships your implementation to every caller and cannot change.

items: Outputs are the module's only public return surface
Anything not declared is unreachable from outside
Root outputs print after apply; `terraform output -json` feeds CI
That JSON is the machine-readable seam — script against it
Consuming a sensitive output requires marking the new one sensitive too
`depends_on` covers side effects missing from the value's graph
Descriptions are registry documentation, not decoration
Output values are computed after apply, not during plan
Feeding one into a caller's `count` or `for_each` throws unknown-value
Fix by moving the branch to a variable or a `-target`ed two-phase apply

left.title: Outputs nothing
items: callers re-query
duplicate data lookups
module hoards knowledge

right.title: Outputs everything
items: internal rename breaks
schema leaks out
major bumps forever
Export IDs and ARNs, not whole resource objects
Whole objects leak schema and break on provider upgrades
Naming: `<resource>_<attribute>`, plural `s` for collections

blocks.title: `terraform_remote_state`
items: Data source reading another root's outputs
Couples two configurations at apply time
Use sparingly, never as a shared database

blocks.title: The Contract
blocks.text: Variables in, outputs out. Change either one and you owe consumers a major version bump — nothing else about the module is public.

items: Local paths must start `./` or `../`, else parsed as a registry address
Registry triple is `<NAMESPACE>/<NAME>/<PROVIDER>`; private adds a host
GitHub shorthand just expands to the HTTPS Git source
Local modules never download and take no `version` argument

lines: # //subdir selects a folder in the repo
# ref takes a tag, branch, or commit SHA

items: SSH form: `git::ssh://git@github.com/acme/tf.git`
Tags are mutable; a commit SHA is the only true pin
`?ref=` is how Git sources version — `version` is ignored

blocks.title: Other Schemes
items: Plain HTTP archive URLs
Local `.zip` files
`source` is never interpolated — init runs before evaluation
No variables, no `locals`, no `format()`, ever
Git credentials come from SSH agent, `.netrc`, `GIT_SSH_COMMAND`
Terraform config holds no credentials for module fetching

blocks.title: Moved Branch
blocks.text: Plain `init` reuses the cached copy. A `?ref=main` source plus no `-upgrade` gives you yesterday's module and today's confidence.

items: Comma-separated terms are ANDed into one range
`~>` floats the last component you wrote — nothing above it
Only providers lock, in `.terraform.lock.hcl`
Loose module constraints drift silently between runs
So: pin exactly in production roots, float in library modules
`>= 3.0, < 4.0` reads clearer than `~>` for humans

blocks.title: Sneaky Break
blocks.text: Adding a required variable with no default deletes nothing, yet every existing caller now fails to plan. That is a MAJOR.

items: `required_version` in a child constrains the whole run's CLI
`required_providers` declares expected providers and ranges
All provider constraints are intersected — one strict child blocks all
Pre-releases like `1.0.0-rc1` are excluded unless asked for exactly

blocks.title: Upgrade Ritual
items: Bump one module version
`terraform plan`, read the whole diff
Commit the pin, then move on
Never bulk-bump five modules
Renovate and Dependabot both parse Terraform module versions
Registry and Git-tag sources only
Local paths and branch refs stay invisible to them
Composition = one module's output into another's input
The reference itself creates the dependency edge
`depends_on` on a `module` makes the whole thing wait
Blunt: it also throws away parallelism you had
Adding `count` later shifts every address underneath
Switching `count` to `for_each` re-creates everything
Unless you write `moved` blocks for each instance
Pass aliases explicitly: `providers = { aws = aws.us_west }`
A module with its own `provider` block cannot use `count` or `for_each`
That shape is a legacy anti-pattern — provider config belongs to the root

left.title: Inversion of control
items: caller builds VPC
module takes IDs
reusable libraries

right.title: Encapsulation
items: module builds all
few inputs
service in a box

blocks.title: Keep It Flat
items: One root calling several focused modules
Three levels deep = unreadable plans
Nesting hides the destroy nobody wanted

blocks.title: Decouple With Lookups
blocks.text: A data source at the caller looking up the VPC by tag beats threading `vpc_id` down through four module layers.

items: One module = one logical unit of infrastructure
Cannot name it in three words? It is two modules
Keep required inputs low — each forces a decision on every caller
Sensible defaults for the 80%, escape hatches for the rest
No option at all for the 1% case
`this` names the module's single primary resource
`locals` hold derived values; never expose one as an override variable
Accept a `tags` map and merge it — never hardcode tags
Never hardcode region, account ID, or environment name

blocks.title: Root's Job, Not Yours
items: No `backend` block in a child
No `provider` block in a child
No workspace names baked in
`examples/` is documentation and the integration test target
`terraform-docs` builds the input/output table from descriptions
Wire it into CI so the docs cannot rot silently

caption.text: Most Terraform pain is not the provider — it is a module with eleven booleans and no version pin. This handbook walks the whole contract: variables in, outputs out, where sources resolve, why `~> 3.1` and `~> 3.1.4` mean different things, and how `moved` blocks let you rename without a destroy. Ten pages, ending with the two checklists that tell you when a module got too clever to keep.
